{{Short description|Probability distribution}}
In the mathematical theory of probability, '''multivariate Laplace distributions''' are extensions of the [[Laplace distribution]] and the [[asymmetric Laplace distribution]] to multiple variables.  The [[marginal distribution]]s of symmetric multivariate Laplace distribution variables are Laplace distributions.  The marginal distributions of asymmetric multivariate Laplace distribution variables are asymmetric Laplace distributions.<ref name=kotz>{{cite book|title=The Laplace Distribution and Generalizations|author1=Kotz. Samuel |author2=Kozubowski, Tomasz J. |author3=Podgorski, Krzysztof |pages=229–245|year=2001|publisher=Birkhauser|isbn=0817641661}}</ref>

==Symmetric multivariate Laplace distribution==
{{Probability distribution
  | name       = Multivariate Laplace (symmetric)
  | type       = multivariate
  | pdf_image  =
  | cdf_image  =
  | notation   =
  | parameters = '''''μ''''' ∈ '''R'''<sup>''k''</sup> — [[location parameter|location]]<br/>'''Σ''' ∈ '''R'''<sup>''k×k''</sup> — [[covariance matrix|covariance]] ([[positive-definite matrix]])
  | support    = '''''x''''' ∈ '''μ''' + span('''Σ''') ⊆ '''R'''<sup>''k''</sup>
  | pdf        = :If <math>\boldsymbol\mu = \mathbf{0}</math>,<br><math>\frac 2 {(2\pi)^{k/2} \left|\boldsymbol\Sigma\right|^{1/2}} \left( \frac {\mathbf{x}'\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1} \mathbf{x}}{2} \right)^{v/2} K_v \left(\sqrt{2\mathbf{x}'\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1} \mathbf{x}} \right), </math><br>where <math>v = (2 - k) / 2</math> and <math>K_v</math> is the [[modified Bessel function of the second kind]].
  <!--- | cdf        = (no analytic expression) --->
  | mean       = '''''μ'''''
  | median     =
  | mode       = '''''μ'''''
  | variance   = '''Σ'''
  | skewness   =0
  | kurtosis   =
  | entropy    =

  | char       = <math> \frac{\exp ( i\boldsymbol\mu'\mathbf{t} )}{1 + \tfrac{1}{2} \mathbf{t}'\boldsymbol\Sigma \mathbf{t} }</math>

A typical characterization of the symmetric multivariate Laplace distribution has the [[Characteristic function (probability theory)|characteristic function]]:

: <math> \varphi(t;\boldsymbol\mu,\boldsymbol\Sigma) = \frac{\exp ( i\boldsymbol\mu'\mathbf{t} )}{1 + \tfrac{1}{2} \mathbf{t}'\boldsymbol\Sigma \mathbf{t}}, </math>

where <math>\boldsymbol\mu</math> is the vector of [[mean]]s for each variable and <math>\boldsymbol\Sigma</math> is the [[covariance matrix]].<ref name=fit>{{cite journal|title=Goodness-of-fit tests for multivariate Laplace distributions|author=Fragiadakis, Konstantinos & Meintanis, Simos G.|journal=Mathematical and Computer Modelling|volume=53|issue=5–6|date=March 2011|pages=769–779|doi=10.1016/j.mcm.2010.10.014|doi-access=free}}</ref>

Unlike the [[multivariate normal distribution]], even if the covariance matrix has zero [[covariance]] and [[correlation]] the variables are not independent.<ref name=kotz/>  The symmetric multivariate Laplace distribution is [[elliptical distribution|elliptical]].<ref name=kotz/>

===Probability density function===
If <math>\boldsymbol\mu = \mathbf{0}</math>, the [[probability density function]] (pdf) for a ''k''-dimensional multivariate Laplace distribution becomes:

:<math> f_{\mathbf x}(x_1,\ldots,x_k) = \frac 2 {(2\pi)^{k/2} |\boldsymbol\Sigma|^{0.5}} \left( \frac {\mathbf{x}'\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1} \mathbf{x}}{2} \right)^{v/2} K_v \left(\sqrt{2\mathbf{x}'\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1} \mathbf{x}} \right), </math>

where:

<math>v = (2 - k) / 2</math> and <math>K_v</math> is the [[modified Bessel function of the second kind]].<ref name=kotz/>

In the correlated bivariate case, i.e., ''k''&nbsp;=&nbsp;2, with <math>\mu_1 = \mu_2 = 0</math> the pdf reduces to:

:<math> f_{\mathbf x}(x_1,x_2) = \frac 1 {\pi \sigma_1 \sigma_2 \sqrt{1-\rho^2}} K_0 \left( \sqrt { \frac { 2 \left( \frac {x_1^2}{\sigma_1^2} - \frac{2 \rho x_1 x_2}{\sigma_1 \sigma_2}  +  \frac {x_2^2}{\sigma_2^2} \right)} { 1-\rho^2 } }  \right),  </math>

where:

<math>\sigma_1</math> and <math>\sigma_2</math> are the [[standard deviation]]s of <math>x_1</math> and <math>x_2</math>, respectively, and <math>\rho</math> is the [[correlation coefficient]] of <math>x_1</math> and <math>x_2</math>.<ref name=kotz/>

For the uncorrelated bivariate Laplace case, that is ''k''&nbsp;=&nbsp;2, <math>\mu_1 = \mu_2 = \rho = 0</math> and <math>\sigma_1 = \sigma_2 = 1</math>, the pdf becomes:

:<math> f_{\mathbf x}(x_1,x_2) = \frac 1 \pi K_0  \left( \sqrt { 2(x_1^2 + x_2^2) } \right).</math><ref name=kotz/>

==Asymmetric multivariate Laplace distribution==
{{Probability distribution
  | name       = Multivariate Laplace (asymmetric)
  | type       = multivariate
  | pdf_image  =
  | cdf_image  =
  | notation   =
  | parameters = '''''μ''''' ∈ '''R'''<sup>''k''</sup> — [[location parameter|location]]<br/>'''Σ''' ∈ '''R'''<sup>''k×k''</sup> — [[covariance matrix|covariance]] ([[positive-definite matrix]])
  | support    = '''''x''''' ∈ '''μ''' + span('''Σ''') ⊆ '''R'''<sup>''k''</sup>
  | pdf        = <math> \frac {2 e^{\mathbf{x}'\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1} \boldsymbol\mu} }{(2\pi)^{\frac{k}{2}} |\boldsymbol\Sigma|^{0.5}} \Big( \frac {\mathbf{x}'\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1} \mathbf{x}}{2 + \boldsymbol\mu'\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1} \boldsymbol\mu} \Big)^\frac{v}{2}  K_v \Big(\sqrt{(2 + \boldsymbol\mu'\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1} \boldsymbol\mu)(\mathbf{x}'\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1} \mathbf{x})} \Big)  </math><br>where <math>v = (2 - k) / 2</math> and <math>K_v</math> is the [[modified Bessel function of the second kind]].
  <!--- | cdf        = (no analytic expression) --->
  | mean       = '''''μ'''''
  | median     =
  | mode       = 
  | variance   = '''Σ''' + '''''μ''''' ' '''''μ'''''
  | skewness   = non-zero unless '''''μ'''''='''0'''
  | kurtosis   =
  | entropy    =
  | mgf        =
  | char       = <math>\frac{1}{1 + \tfrac{1}{2} \mathbf{t}'\boldsymbol\Sigma \mathbf{t} - i\boldsymbol\mu\mathbf{t} }</math>
  }}

A typical characterization of the asymmetric multivariate Laplace distribution has the [[characteristic function (probability theory)|characteristic function]]:

: <math> \varphi(t;\boldsymbol\mu,\boldsymbol\Sigma) = \frac{1}{1 + \tfrac{1}{2} \mathbf{t}'\boldsymbol\Sigma \mathbf{t} - i\boldsymbol\mu\mathbf{t} }. </math><ref name=kotz/>

As with the symmetric multivariate Laplace distribution, the asymmetric multivariate Laplace distribution has mean <math>\boldsymbol\mu</math>, but the covariance becomes <math>\boldsymbol\Sigma + \boldsymbol\mu'\boldsymbol\mu</math>.<ref name=multi>{{cite journal|title=Multivariate Generalized Laplace Distributions and Related Random Fields|author1=Kozubowski, Tomasz J. |author2=Podgorski, Krzysztof |author3=Rychlik, Igor |journal=Journal of Multivariate Analysis |publisher=University of Gothenburg|year=2010|volume=113 |pages=59–72 |doi=10.1016/j.jmva.2012.02.010 |s2cid=206252976 |doi-access=free }}</ref>  The asymmetric multivariate Laplace distribution is not elliptical unless <math>\boldsymbol\mu = \mathbf{0}</math>, in which case the distribution reduces to the symmetric multivariate Laplace distribution with <math>\boldsymbol\mu = \mathbf{0}</math>.<ref name=kotz/>

The [[probability density function]] (pdf) for a ''k''-dimensional asymmetric multivariate Laplace distribution is:

:<math> f_{\mathbf x}(x_1,\ldots,x_k) = \frac {2 e^{\mathbf{x}'\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1} \boldsymbol\mu} }{(2\pi)^{k/2} |\boldsymbol\Sigma|^{0.5}} \Big( \frac {\mathbf{x}'\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1} \mathbf{x}}{2 + \boldsymbol\mu'\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1} \boldsymbol\mu} \Big)^{v/2}  K_v \Big(\sqrt{(2 + \boldsymbol\mu'\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1} \boldsymbol\mu)(\mathbf{x}'\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1} \mathbf{x})} \Big), </math>

where:

<math>v = (2 - k) / 2</math> and <math>K_v</math> is the [[modified Bessel function of the second kind]].<ref name=kotz/>

The asymmetric Laplace distribution, including the special case of <math>\boldsymbol\mu = \mathbf{0}</math>, is an example of a [[geometric stable distribution]].<ref name=multi/>  It represents the limiting distribution for a sum of [[independent, identically distributed random variables]] with finite variance and covariance where the number of elements to be summed is itself an independent random variable distributed according to a [[geometric distribution]].<ref name=kotz/>  Such geometric sums can arise in practical applications within biology, economics and insurance.<ref name=kotz/>  The distribution may also be applicable in broader situations to model multivariate data with heavier tails than a normal distribution but finite [[moment (mathematics)|moments]].<ref name=kotz/>

The relationship between the [[exponential distribution]] and the [[Laplace distribution]] allows for a simple method for simulating bivariate asymmetric Laplace variables (including for the case of <math>\boldsymbol\mu = \mathbf{0}</math>).  Simulate a bivariate normal random variable vector <math>\mathbf{Y}</math> from a distribution with <math>\mu_1=\mu_2=0</math> and covariance matrix  <math>\boldsymbol\Sigma</math>.  Independently simulate an exponential random variable <math>\mathbf{W}</math> from an Exp(1) distribution. <math>\mathbf{X} = \sqrt{W} \mathbf{Y} + W \boldsymbol\mu </math> will be distributed (asymmetric) bivariate Laplace with mean <math>\boldsymbol\mu</math> and covariance matrix <math>\boldsymbol\Sigma</math>.<ref name=kotz/>
